title: Poulet à l'Estragon
subtitle: Chicken braised in white wine and cream with fresh tarragon
excerpt: Chicken thighs braised with white wine, cream, and a large bunch of tarragon. The sauce is lightly herb-scented and silky, cooked in a single pan in about 40 minutes.
sourceNotes: Poulet à l'estragon is a classic of the French bourgeois kitchen. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), chicken with tarragon chapter. Fernand Point, Ma Gastronomie (1969), whose restaurant La Pyramide was famous for a version of this dish. Tarragon is the herb most closely identified with classic French chicken cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: An aromatic herb with a mild anise flavour, widely used in French cooking. French tarragon (as opposed to Russian tarragon) has the stronger, more refined flavour that the classic recipes call for.

content.text: Poulet à l'estragon is chicken in a white wine and cream sauce scented with

. The herb goes in twice: a few sprigs braise with the chicken to flavour the sauce, and fresh leaves are added at the end to keep the green colour and the bright anise note. The result is a silky, lightly herb-scented sauce that works equally well for a quick weeknight dinner or a dinner table.

Season the chicken thighs with salt and pepper. Heat the butter and oil in a wide sauté pan over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken, skin-side down, for 5 minutes until golden. Turn and cook 2 minutes more. Remove and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Add the shallots and cook for 4 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the wine and stock. Add the tarragon sprigs. Bring to a simmer and cook for 3 minutes.
Return the chicken to the pan, skin-side up. Cover and cook over low heat for 20 minutes until cooked through.

Remove the chicken. Fish out and discard the tarragon sprigs. Pour the cream into the pan and simmer for 3 to 4 minutes until the sauce coats the back of a spoon. Stir in the fresh tarragon leaves. Taste and season. Return the chicken to the pan and serve.

items.cause: Not enough fresh tarragon at the end, or the herb was added too early.
items.fix: Add more fresh tarragon leaves just before serving. The green, anise flavour of tarragon dissipates with heat; keeping the finishing addition off-heat or at the last moment preserves it.

items.symptom: The cream sauce is too thin
items.cause: The cream was not reduced long enough after the chicken was removed.
items.fix: Simmer the sauce for a further 2 to 3 minutes. It should coat the back of a spoon before you return the chicken. A good sauce at this stage clings to the chicken when plated.

items.symptom: The chicken skin is not golden
items.cause: The pan was not hot enough when the chicken went in.
items.fix: Make sure the butter-oil mixture is very hot before the chicken goes in, skin-side down. A proper sizzle on contact means the skin is already setting.

items.symptom: The sauce has a slightly bitter finish
items.cause: The tarragon sprigs cooked for too long in the hot sauce.
items.fix: Remove the sprigs after the braising stage, before the cream goes in. Only the fresh leaves go in at the end.

content.text: Tarragon is one of the four fines herbes of French classical cooking, alongside chives, chervil, and parsley. Its affinity for chicken is so strong that the pairing appears across almost every region of France and in every level of French cooking, from home kitchens to three-star restaurants. Fernand Point, whose restaurant La Pyramide in Vienne was one of the most influential in 20th-century France, was especially associated with the dish. It remains one of the most imitated of French chicken preparations.
